title: AI chatbots are becoming a low-cost health-navigation layer while usefulness, privacy, and mental-health legitimacy remain unsettled
source_unit: Pew Research Center, From Diagnoses to Treatments, Why Americans Use AI Chatbots for Health, and companion analysis on loneliness, depression, and stress, August 25, 2026
geography: United States; adults nationally with health-chatbot use, age, race/ethnicity, income, education, AI-attitude, helpfulness, privacy, and mental-health judgments

observations.period: June 22-28, 2026; reasons for using AI chatbots for health

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew American Trends Panel survey

any_health_chatbot_use.unit: percent ever using AI chatbots for at least one of eight health or medical reasons

quick_information.unit: percent using chatbots to get health information quickly

figure_out_symptoms.unit: percent using chatbots to figure out what is causing symptoms

low_or_no_cost.unit: percent using chatbots to get health information at little or no cost

understand_doctor_diagnosis.unit: percent using chatbots to learn more about a diagnosis from a doctor

understand_lab_results.unit: percent using chatbots to help understand lab results

uncomfortable_topics.unit: percent using chatbots for health information they are uncomfortable talking about

decide_whether_to_see_doctor.unit: percent using chatbots to help decide whether to go to a doctor

observations.method: Pew survey of 3,488 U.S. adults conducted June 22-28, 2026; respondents were members of the American Trends Panel and the survey represents U.S. adults.
observations.uncertainty: The survey measures ever-use and stated reasons, not frequency, clinical accuracy, actual cost savings, medical urgency, or whether chatbot use replaced or complemented a clinician.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with reason-specific measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Chatbots may be serving as a translation, preparation, and question-formulation layer around clinical care rather than a wholesale substitute for it; low cost and discomfort may still indicate unmet access.

observations.period: June 2026; demographic and attitudinal concentration of chatbot health use

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew survey; subgroup estimates use weighted universes

asian_chatbot_health_users.unit: percent of Asian adults; English-speaker estimate

age_65_plus_users.unit: percent of adults ages 65 and older

excited_about_ai_users.unit: percent among adults who say increased AI use makes them more excited

concerned_about_ai_users.unit: percent among adults who say increased AI use makes them more concerned

observations.method: Pew weighted demographic and AI-attitude comparisons for the health-chatbot-user measure.
observations.uncertainty: These are associations and do not show whether income, age, education, race/ethnicity, optimism, or access caused the different use rates; Asian estimates represent English speakers.
observations.subgroup: Adults by race/ethnicity, age, education, family income, and attitude toward AI.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher use among younger, wealthier, and more AI-positive groups may reflect overall chatbot familiarity and resources, while lower use may represent trust, access, language, or digital-skill barriers.

observations.period: June 2026; perceived usefulness and health-data privacy

denominator.unit: U.S. adults who ever use AI chatbots for at least one health or medical reason; conditional denominator

extremely_very_helpful.unit: percent of chatbot health users finding information extremely or very helpful

not_helpful.unit: percent of chatbot health users finding information not too or not at all helpful

very_extremely_comfortable_sharing_healt.unit: percent of chatbot health users very or extremely comfortable sharing personal health information

somewhat_comfortable.unit: percent of chatbot health users somewhat comfortable

not_comfortable.unit: percent of chatbot health users not too or not at all comfortable

observations.method: Pew conditional measures among adults who use chatbots for health, asking separately about perceived helpfulness and comfort sharing personal health information.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived helpfulness is not clinical benefit, and comfort is not informed consent, actual disclosure, privacy protection, or data-governance compliance.
observations.subgroup: Adults who use AI chatbots for health or medical reasons.
observations.counterinterpretation: A useful tool can remain privacy-sensitive: the middle-heavy comfort distribution suggests adoption may depend on bounded disclosure, platform trust, and clarity about storage and secondary use.

observations.period: June 2026; public judgments of chatbots for loneliness, depression, and stress

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew survey; companion analysis uses same survey

loneliness_hurt.unit: percent saying chatbots do more to hurt people using them for loneliness support

loneliness_help.unit: percent saying chatbots do more to help

depression_hurt.unit: percent saying chatbots do more to hurt people using them for depression support

depression_help.unit: percent saying chatbots do more to help

stress_hurt.unit: percent saying chatbots do more to hurt people using them for stress support

stress_help.unit: percent saying chatbots do more to help

older_adults_unsure_loneliness.unit: percent of adults 65+ unsure whether chatbots help or hurt for loneliness support

observations.method: Pew companion analysis using the same June 22-28, 2026 survey, with age and race/ethnicity comparisons for perceived effects of chatbots on social and mental health support.
observations.uncertainty: These are public judgments about possible effects, not clinical evaluations or reports of users' outcomes; uncertainty is substantial and varies by age and race/ethnicity.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults nationally, with age and race/ethnicity comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: The public may distinguish information/navigation uses from relational or mental-health support uses: utility is easier to accept when the tool supplements care, while social substitution triggers more concern.

related_sources.title: From Diagnoses to Treatments, Why Americans Use AI Chatbots for Health

boundary: This record adds an AI-mediated health-navigation and social-support layer: speed, cost, privacy, diagnostic interpretation, sensitive questions, and emotional support create different legitimacy conditions. It does not establish clinical accuracy, treatment efficacy, data protection, mental-health outcomes, or whether chatbot use replaces professional care.
